Was the change abrupt? A step against a ramp, at every changepoint

Source: R/abruptness.R
cpt_abruptness.Rd

For each changepoint of a change in mean, fits the window around it (between the neighbouring changepoints) twice: as a step, which is what every detector assumes, and as a linear ramp from the old level to the new one, with its centre and width estimated. When the ramp fits clearly better, the change took time, and the reported location is the middle of a transition rather than a moment.

Usage

cpt_abruptness(fit, level = 0.95, max_width = NULL)

# S3 method for class 'ggcpt_abruptness'
print(x, ...)

# S3 method for class 'ggcpt_abruptness'
tidy(x, ...)

# S3 method for class 'ggcpt_abruptness'
autoplot(object, ...)

Arguments

fit

A ggcpt object with a change in mean (or mean and variance).

level

Level of the interval for the transition width, and 1 - level the threshold at which the step is rejected. Defaults to 0.95.

max_width

Widest ramp considered, in observations. Defaults to half the window.

x

A ggcpt_abruptness object.

...

Ignored.

object

A ggcpt_abruptness object.

Value

A ggcpt_abruptness tibble with one row per changepoint: cp, window_start, window_end, width (the best ramp width, in observations), width_lower and width_upper (its interval), centre (the ramp's centre), statistic (the likelihood-ratio statistic against the step), p_value and verdict ("abrupt" when the step is not rejected, "gradual" when it is). autoplot() draws each window with the step and the ramp; print() and tidy() work as usual.

How it decides

For a ramp of width \(w\) centred at \(c\), the level is \(a\) before \(c - w/2\), \(b\) after \(c + w/2\), and linear between, so for fixed \((c, w)\) the fit is ordinary least squares in \((a, b)\). The residual sum of squares is profiled over the centre for each width on a grid (every width up to 8, then geometric), and the step is the width-0 member of the family. The statistic \(m \log(RSS_{step} / RSS_{ramp})\) over the window's \(m\) observations is compared with a chi-squared distribution on one degree of freedom. The step sits on the boundary of the family, which makes that reference conservative, and the search over widths and centres, which makes it liberal; measured on true steps (jumps of 1 to 8 noise standard deviations, \(n\) of 300 and 1,000, Gaussian and \(t_3\) noise, 400 replicates each, detected with pelt), the step was rejected in 1.0 to 5.2 per cent of fits at level = 0.95. A ramp of 2 standard deviations over 30 observations was called gradual in 53 per cent of fits at \(n = 300\), over 60 observations in 70 per cent. The width interval collects every width whose profile statistic is within the chi-squared quantile of the best.

A ramp also fits a step plus a few outliers near it, and a window that holds a second, undetected change; read "gradual" as "a step is not an adequate description", and look at autoplot().

See also

cpt_simulate() with transition, to measure how a detector places a gradual change; cpt_gof().

Other inference: cpt_assumptions(), cpt_attribute(), cpt_attribute_event(), cpt_confint_coverage(), cpt_effect(), cpt_gof(), cpt_k_weights(), cpt_null_power(), cpt_robustness(), cpt_screen(), cpt_test_at(), cpt_test_null()

Examples

set.seed(2026)
ramp <- c(rep(0, 100), seq(0, 4, length.out = 30), rep(4, 100))
fit <- cpt_detect(ramp + rnorm(230, 0, 0.5), method = "pelt")
cpt_abruptness(fit)
#> ggcpt_abruptness (a step against a ramp at each changepoint)
#>   Changepoint 116:    gradual, transition width 24 (24 to 31)
#> 
#> # A tibble: 1 × 10
#>      cp window_start window_end width width_lower width_upper centre statistic
#>   <int>        <int>      <int> <dbl>       <dbl>       <dbl>  <dbl>     <dbl>
#> 1   116            1        230    24          24          31    115      82.2
#> # ℹ 2 more variables: p_value <dbl>, verdict <chr>
step <- cpt_detect(c(rnorm(100), rnorm(100, 4)), method = "pelt")
cpt_abruptness(step)
#> ggcpt_abruptness (a step against a ramp at each changepoint)
#>   Changepoint 100:    gradual, transition width 3 (1 to 16)
#> 
#> # A tibble: 1 × 10
#>      cp window_start window_end width width_lower width_upper centre statistic
#>   <int>        <int>      <int> <dbl>       <dbl>       <dbl>  <dbl>     <dbl>
#> 1   100            1        200     3           1          16    100      4.43
#> # ℹ 2 more variables: p_value <dbl>, verdict <chr>
